921.event_title: General Mahabat Khan seizes the heavy-drinking Emperor Jahangir on the Jhelum
921.place: Imperial camp on the Jhelum River, Mughal Empire (now Pakistan)
921.event: The Mughal emperor Jahangir was a heavy drinker and opium user who, even in the settled middle years of his reign, kept a court official whose charge was the care of the imperial intoxicants. In March 1626 the general Mahabat Khan, summoned to court to answer charges, arrived at the imperial camp on the Jhelum River with about 5,000 Rajput soldiers and, finding the imperial household isolated on one bank, took the emperor captive. Nur Jahan's attempt to rescue her husband failed, and the royal couple remained in Mahabat Khan's hands for months before they managed to slip free later that year.
921.explanation: An emperor of the richest state in South Asia was seized in his own camp by one of his own commanders, a public humiliation that showed how little awe the throne then commanded.
921.tie_back: The kural warns that those who live in love with drink are not feared by their enemies and lose their lustre, and the habitually intoxicated Jahangir was captured by his own general and had to be rescued by his wife.
921._accuracy_note: Jahangir's long dependence on wine and opium and his capture are both well documented, but the sources do not say his drinking caused the coup, so the fit rests on the pairing rather than proven cause.

922.event_title: Babur publicly renounces wine before the Battle of Khanwa
922.place: Near Sikri and Khanwa, northern India
922.event: As the Rajput confederacy under Rana Sanga of Mewar advanced against him, and his men were losing heart after early setbacks, the Mughal founder Babur publicly forswore wine, which had been one of the great pleasures of his life. About 300 of his nobles and household joined him in the vow, and he also declared the coming fight a holy war, with his men swearing on the Quran not to turn back. Babur then defeated Rana Sanga's much larger army at Khanwa in March 1527, a victory that secured Mughal rule in northern India.
922.explanation: At the moment when he most needed the trust and respect of his followers, Babur chose to give up drink openly, and the gesture was part of what restored his army's morale.
922.tie_back: The kural bids people not to drink, leaving liquor only to those who do not care for the esteem of the worthy, and Babur gave up wine precisely when he needed the respect of the men who would follow him into battle.
922._accuracy_note: A clear, documented act of renouncing liquor for the sake of standing and leadership; the kural's ironic point about those indifferent to the esteem of the wise is matched only from the positive side.

923.event_title: The Women's Crusade against the saloons begins at Hillsboro, Ohio
923.event: After the lecturer Dio Lewis told audiences how his own mother had prayed with other wives of drinking men until a saloon keeper closed his business, women in Hillsboro, Ohio, formed a committee led by Eliza Jane Thompson and from 26 December 1873 went into saloons and drug stores to pray, sing and ask sellers to sign pledges to stop selling liquor. Similar bands spread across the Midwest and Northeast in the winter of 1873-74, drawing tens of thousands of women, most of whom had until then confined themselves to the roles of wives and mothers. The movement led directly to the founding of the Woman's Christian Temperance Union in Cleveland in November 1874.
923.explanation: The Crusade showed how deeply drunkenness wounded the women closest to drinkers, enough to bring wives and mothers out of their homes into public protest for the first time on such a scale.
923.tie_back: The kural says that drunkenness is painful to see even for a mother, the most forgiving of witnesses, and the Women's Crusade was born from the grief of mothers and wives watching the men of their families drink.
923._accuracy_note: Captures the pain drink causes to mothers and families, but the kural's argument from a mother's forbearance to the stricter judgement of the wise is not directly illustrated.

924.event_title: Andrew Johnson's intoxicated vice-presidential inaugural speech
924.place: Senate Chamber, United States Capitol, Washington, D.C., United States
924.event: Before being sworn in as vice president, Andrew Johnson, who had spent the previous evening drinking and reportedly took three glasses of whiskey that morning against fatigue and a cold, rose to address a Senate Chamber filled with senators, justices, diplomats and President Lincoln. He rambled for about twenty minutes about his humble origins, ignored outgoing vice president Hannibal Hamlin's tugs on his coat, and was too disoriented to swear in the new senators, a task a clerk completed. Senators were mortified, reporters wired the story across the country, and both Massachusetts senators introduced a resolution calling for his resignation.
924.explanation: In one morning of drink a man about to stand next in line for the presidency publicly shamed himself before the nation's leaders.
924.tie_back: The kural says the noble lady Modesty turns her back on those who drink, and on that morning Johnson's sense of shame deserted him in front of the whole Senate.
924._accuracy_note: Close to a dramatisation of drink driving out modesty and decorum in public; the episode was a single lapse rather than the habitual drinking the kural has in view.

925.event_title: Hogarth's Gin Lane and the Gin Act end London's Gin Craze
925.event: In the first half of the eighteenth century cheap, unlicensed gin became so widely sold in London that by 1723 Londoners were estimated to drink on average a pint a week, and people addicted to it spent their wages on drink and sold or pawned their possessions to buy more. In 1751 William Hogarth published Gin Lane, set in St Giles, where a sign over a gin cellar advertised that a customer could be drunk for a penny and dead drunk for twopence, and where the pawnbroker, distiller and undertaker thrive while the poor decay. The print supported the Gin Act of 1751, which restricted who could sell gin and raised its cost, after which gin drinking declined.
925.explanation: The Gin Craze is a famous case of a whole city paying away its earnings and goods to buy oblivion.
925.tie_back: The kural mocks those who pay good money to buy a state in which they no longer know themselves, and the gin sellers of St Giles literally priced unconsciousness at a penny or twopence.
925._accuracy_note: The penny and twopence sign is almost the kural itself; the event is a social crisis rather than one individual's folly.

926.event_title: Repin paints the dying Modest Mussorgsky
926.event: After the triumphs of Boris Godunov and Pictures at an Exhibition in 1874, the composer Modest Mussorgsky fell into drinking bouts in St Petersburg taverns that could last for days, and his worsening alcoholism eventually made him unemployable in the government posts that supported him. In early 1881 he was hospitalised with chronic alcoholism, and the collector Pavel Tretyakov sent Ilya Repin to paint him; Repin's red-nosed portrait, made over a few sittings, now hangs in the Tretyakov Gallery. Mussorgsky died on 28 March 1881, aged only forty-two, before Repin could return for a final sitting.
926.explanation: One of Russia's most original composers was destroyed by drink at forty-two, and the portrait painted in his last days became one of the most famous images of a ruined genius.
926.tie_back: The kural says that drinkers are no different from those who swallow poison, and Mussorgsky's drinking worked on him like a slow poison that killed him in his prime.
926._accuracy_note: A well-documented death from alcoholism that bears out the poison comparison; the kural's further parallel between sleep and death is not illustrated.

927.event_title: George Cassiday, the Man in the Green Hat, exposes Congress's secret drinking
927.place: United States Capitol, Washington, D.C., United States
927.event: Throughout Prohibition, a bootlegger named George Cassiday quietly delivered liquor in a leather briefcase to the offices of members of the House and Senate, beginning with two House members who had voted for Prohibition. After a 1925 arrest in the House office building made him famous as the Man in the Green Hat, he moved his trade to the Senate side, until Prohibition agents caught him with six bottles of gin in the senators' parking lot on 18 February 1930. He then wrote a front-page series for the Washington Post describing how he had helped about 80 percent of lawmakers break the law, and senators demanded in vain that his client list be published to clear their names.
927.explanation: Lawmakers who publicly supported Prohibition while drinking in private became a national symbol of hypocrisy once their supplier told his story.
927.tie_back: The kural warns that those who drink in secret will have their secret found out and be laughed at by their own townspeople, and Congress's hidden drinking was exposed and mocked across the nation.
927._accuracy_note: A close match to secret drinking being exposed and ridiculed; the exposure came from the bootlegger rather than from neighbours prying, and no individual drinkers were named.

928.event_title: Cleitus speaks his grievances at a drinking party and is killed by Alexander
928.event: At a banquet in Maracanda, the officer Cleitus, who had saved Alexander's life at the Granicus and had just been named governor of Bactria, heard courtiers flatter Alexander at the expense of his father Philip and the older generation of commanders. Heated with wine, Cleitus answered with insolent words, praising Philip and saying that soldiers win the victories for which generals take the glory. Alexander, also in a drunken rage, seized a weapon and killed him, and when sober again was overcome with remorse for days.
928.explanation: Wine drew out resentments that Cleitus had kept to himself and stripped away the restraint of both men, turning a feast into a tragedy that Alexander bitterly regretted.
928.tie_back: The kural warns that the moment a man drinks, whatever he has hidden in his heart comes out all the more, as Cleitus's long-held grievances burst out at the drinking party.
928._accuracy_note: Ancient sources differ in detail but agree that drink brought hidden resentment into the open; the kural's specific target, the drinker who denies his drinking, is not present.

929.event_title: The Bronte family fails to rescue Branwell Bronte from drink
929.event: After he was dismissed from his post as a tutor at Thorp Green in July 1845, Branwell Bronte, the only brother of Charlotte, Emily and Anne, returned to Haworth and over the next three years sank into dependence on alcohol and opium. His family's distress is recorded in Charlotte's letters, the local doctor recommended only that he abstain from alcohol, and in his last year his father, the Reverend Patrick Bronte, took him into his own room to watch over him at night. Branwell's health collapsed and he died on 24 September 1848, aged thirty-one, probably of tuberculosis.
929.explanation: A family of exceptional intelligence and devotion could neither argue nor watch Branwell out of his addiction.
929.tie_back: The kural compares reasoning with a drunkard to searching with a torch for someone sunk deep under water, and all the advice and care of Branwell's family could not reach him.
929._accuracy_note: The sources document the family's distress and attempts at control rather than specific reasoned appeals, so the fit to futile reasoning is partial.

930.event_title: Bill Wilson seeks out a fellow alcoholic in Akron and Alcoholics Anonymous begins
930.event: Bill Wilson, a New York stockbroker who had stopped drinking after a hospital stay in late 1934, found himself alone and tempted to drink in an Akron hotel in 1935 after a business deal failed. Having learned that talking with other alcoholics kept him sober, he telephoned a local clergyman and was put in touch with Robert Smith, a physician who was still drinking, and Wilson stayed on in Smith's house for several months. Smith stopped drinking soon after, and the two men's work with other alcoholics grew into Alcoholics Anonymous.
930.explanation: Wilson discovered that facing another drinker's condition was what kept him from returning to his own, and that insight became the basis of a worldwide movement.
930.tie_back: The kural asks whether a sober drinker, seeing another man drunk, does not recognise his own state when drinking, and Wilson kept himself sober precisely by seeing his own condition in another alcoholic.
930._accuracy_note: A strong illustration of self-recognition through another drinker; the founding of AA already appears once elsewhere in the book, and here Smith was a struggling drinker rather than a reeling drunk.
